Kevin Rideout was kidnapped in Niger’s capital and no armed group claimed responsibility for the abduction. Photograph: Issouf Sanogo/AFP/Getty Images Niger American missionary kidnapped in Niger freed after nine months Kevin Rideout, who was abducted by unknown assailants in Niamey, said to be in good health and in care of US officials Associated Press in Niamey Fri 14 Aug 2026 05.48 EDT Last modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 05.58 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An American missionary who was kidnapped in Niger in October has been released, his organisation has said. Kevin Rideout “is in good health in the care of US officials” and would soon be reunited with his extended family, SIM International said in a statement. Rideout was kidnapped in the west African country’s capital, Niamey, on 21 October by three armed individuals and was probably driven out of town, according to a security official at the time. No armed group claimed responsibility for the abduction. Niger has long been the target of attacks by armed groups, including jihadis linked to al-Qaida and Islamic State. The US embassy in Niamey issued a security alert a day after Rideout’s abduction, warning that American citizens “remain at a heightened risk of kidnapping throughout Niger, including in the capital city”. Niger is ruled by a military junta that took power in 2023 after deposing the democratically elected president, Mohamed Bazoum. The new authorities ousted western partners, including the US, which had soldiers in Niger, and forged a new security and diplomatic alliance with Russia. In June, more than 30 people were killed when gunmen attacked the main airport in Niamey. It was the second attack this year at the airport , a strategic hub that serves as the ruling military’s command, hosting its air force base and most of its drones and aircraft. It is also the headquarters of the regional alliance that brings together troops from Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso. The violence is the latest sign of armed groups increasingly targeting cities and urban centres in Africa’s Sahel region. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj03.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Farm workers rely on boats to get to rice fields and to transport goods By Makuochi Okafor ,Â West Africa Reporter Â and Â Ruth Comerford Published 4 hours ago At least 46 people have died in Nigeria after a boat capsized in north-western Sokoto state. The boat was believed to be carrying more than 70 people, mostly children, and a search operation is ongoing, officials say. Police spokesperson Ahmad Rufai told the BBC on Thursday that 46 bodies had been found near Gorau in Gorony. Sixteen people have been recovered safely, while 15 are still missing. The area is difficult to reach, and security agencies and emergency services are heading to the site, Rufai added. One witness told the Reuters news agency he believed the children on board were travelling with farm owners and labourers who were heading to work on a rice harvest. The witness said they saw saw 50 bodies, many wrapped in âmats and traditional cloths, lying in the front of a community mosque ahead of their âburial. Nigeria's emergency management agency (Nema) spokesperson Ezekiel Manzo told the BBC that "Gorau is a very remote place... the team has moved to that remote location. Boat accidents are common in Nigeria, with overcrowding, poorly maintained boats and weak enforcement of safety rules often blamed for deaths. At least five people drowned when a boat overturned in Jigawa state last month . In January, at least 26 people drowned when a boat carrying farmers and fishermen from Jigawa to Yobe state capsized. And in December 2024, 54 bodies were recovered from the River Niger after a boat that may have been carrying more than 200 passengers capsized. Authorities have recommended measures including providing safer boats and life jackets, dredging waterways, deploying water guards at jetties and terminals, and ensuring boat operators are properly trained and licensed. But many of these measures have not been fully implemented or properly enforced. For millions of Nigerians, particularly in rural communities, rivers are an important means of transport. Many villages are located near waterways, while poor roads and a lack of bridges can make travel by land difficult. Wooden boats are often used to transport people and goods, including to markets and neighbouring communities. https://www.politico.eu/article/donald-t.text: DOONBEG, Ireland — U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday called on Ukraine to stop targeting Russian oil refineries in light of the surging price of diesel fuel worldwide. Trump, who is on a two-day visit to Ireland , made the remarks to reporters while walking around his golf course in County Clare, which is hosting the Irish Open tournament. Asked about the current surge in global fuel prices, particularly diesel — which broke a record $6 per gallon in the U.S. on Friday — Trump insisted the spike was being caused by Ukraine rather than his own war with Iran, which has sharply restricted oil shipments from the Middle East. Advertisement Advertisement Trump said officials from his administration had asked Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop drone and missile attacks on any Russian sites that produce diesel. “Mr Zelenskyy has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” Trump said during a pause on his tour of his Doonbeg golf course on Ireland’s west coast. “Let him go after targets but not diesel fuel, because he’s causing a shortage of diesel fuel.” The U.S. leader maintained that the conflict Washington initiated with Iran more than six months ago is not to blame for the shortfall. “This isn’t done by the Middle East,” Trump said. “This is done by what’s happening with Russia and Ukraine. So we spoke to Mr Zelenskyy about it. There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel, because that’s hurting the world.” Ukraine’s increasingly deep-range strikes on Russian energy infrastructure are seen as a key part of its strategy to make Russia’s 4-year full-scale invasion of the country prohibitively costly for Moscow. But a senior European official familiar with U.S.-brokered mediation talks between Moscow and Kyiv told POLITICO that the Trump administration was searching for scapegoats ahead of crucial Nov. 3 midterm elections in the United States. The official was granted anonymity to comment on sensitive aspects of the three-way discussions. “This administration is blaming Ukraine because they do not know what to do with their war [in Iran],” the official said. “Russian exports of diesel and oil have never been significant for U.S. consumption. The very idea is absurd. Moreover, we have all heard President Trump say that America itself can supply as much oil as anyone wants.” Advertisement Advertisement Trump is not the first U.S. official to blame Ukrainian strikes for the price of diesel. Last week, Energy Secretary Chris Wright told CBS that “the diesel situation has been challenging because Russian refineries have suffered significant damage.” Days before that, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told the “Fox & Friends” program that America was experiencing “an energy shock” partly because “Ukraine has decided that they want to blow up Russian energy assets and refined properties.” The senior European official said that if Washington wanted Kyiv to stop attacking Russian refineries, it should get Moscow to stop hitting Ukraine’s energy grid. “An energy ceasefire must be mutual,” the official said. “Putin does not respect this [U.S.] administration. That is why a ceasefire hasn’t begun.” Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told the Vesti news service on Saturday that Moscow would not pause its attacks during the talks with Kyiv. “We remain ready for negotiations, but the special military operation will not be halted for the duration of the talks. We have already been through this experience and drawn our own conclusions.” Veronika Melkozerova in Kyiv contributed reporting to this story.

https://baltic-review.com/estonia-pisa-2.text: Share Tweet 0 Estonia’s latest international education results show strong performance in science and mathematics alongside a continuing focus on reading skills. A strong result with a clear next task Estonia’s 15-year-old students remain among Europe’s strongest performers in the latest Programme for International Student Assessment, or PISA, results published on Tuesday, September 8. The country ranked first in Europe in both science and mathematics and second in reading, according to Estonia’s Ministry of Education and Research. The results offer a broadly positive picture of attainment while also pointing to areas where schools and policymakers will need to concentrate attention. PISA is organised by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development and assesses students around the age of 15 in science, mathematics and reading. The 2025 cycle placed particular emphasis on science and also examined computational problem-solving and aspects of learning in a digital environment. In Estonia, 6,304 students from 204 schools took part, representing approximately 14,600 15-year-olds nationwide. ([oecd.org](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/pisa-2025-results-volume-i-country-notes_2d4ff9ea-en/estonia_3b256c6a-en.html)) Science remains Estonia’s leading strength The Estonian ministry reported an average score of 508 points in mathematics and 499 points in reading. In science, Estonia was the highest-performing European participant and sixth among all participating countries and education systems. Around 90% of Estonian students reached at least the basic proficiency level in science, while 11.3% were top performers. The OECD’s country note confirms that Estonian students performed above the OECD average in all three core subjects, as well as in computational problem-solving. Approximately 90% reached the baseline level in science, compared with 74% across the OECD. In mathematics and reading, 83% of students reached at least Level 2, compared with OECD averages of 65% and 69% respectively. ([oecd.org](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/pisa-2025-results-volume-i-country-notes_2d4ff9ea-en/estonia_3b256c6a-en.html)) These figures matter because the PISA baseline is intended to represent practical competence rather than specialist achievement. At Level 2 in science, students can recognise explanations for familiar phenomena and use supplied data to judge whether a conclusion is valid. In mathematics, they can interpret simple situations and represent them mathematically. In reading, they can identify a main idea, locate information and reflect on a text’s purpose when guided to do so. Reading performance remains the main concern The results are not uniformly positive. The OECD found that Estonia’s 2025 average was broadly unchanged from 2022 in science and mathematics, but lower in reading. The ministry reported that Estonia’s reading score was just one point behind Ireland, which led Europe in the subject. At the same time, reading performance has declined over the longer term: the ministry said Estonia’s score was 15 points lower than a decade earlier, while the OECD recorded a rise in the share of students below the basic reading level compared with 2015. That trend gives the results a more useful interpretation than a simple league table. Estonia has retained a broad base of students able to meet minimum standards, but the country must also consider how reading habits, concentration, digital media and the ability to assess information are changing. The education ministry said reading comprehension is becoming more important as students encounter artificial intelligence and increasingly complex information environments. Evidence of confidence and pressure inside schools The survey also provides information about how young people experience learning. Eighty-three percent of Estonian students said they believe their abilities can develop through effort and learning, a measure the OECD describes as a growth mindset. Many students also reported turning to teachers and classmates when they need help. At the same time, the OECD identified pressures within the school environment. A larger share of Estonian students than in 2022 attended schools where principals said shortages of educational materials hindered teaching to some extent. Teacher availability was another concern in the national summary. The findings therefore combine strong student performance with practical questions about staffing, learning materials and the capacity of schools to support different learners. A basis for the next phase of education policy For Estonia, the new PISA results provide both recognition and direction. The country’s science and mathematics performance suggests that its schools are continuing to give many students a strong foundation in analytical subjects. The relatively high proportion reaching minimum standards also indicates that achievement is not limited to a small elite. The next challenge is to protect that breadth while strengthening reading. That could mean closer attention to sustained reading, comprehension across subjects and the critical evaluation of online information, alongside continued support for teachers and school resources. PISA cannot explain every reason behind a result, and it is not a substitute for classroom-level assessment. It can, however, help identify where a high-performing education system should focus its next improvements.
